_meta.purpose: Step 12, #139 — proves the minmax_subquery check in src/nl2sql/pipeline/soundness.py. Selecting the row that owns an extreme value via an equality against a scalar MIN/MAX subquery is the shape ORDER BY x LIMIT 1 expresses more reliably; flagged as a correction signal (diagnostic-grade).
_meta.format: (candidate SQL, expected verdict) pairs; 'flag' → soundness hit, 'pass' → clean. See null_ordering.json for the catch-rate / false-positive semantics.
_meta.rule: Only an UNCORRELATED scalar MIN/MAX subquery (no WHERE of its own that could reference the outer row) matched by '=' is flagged. A correlated subquery genuinely needs the subquery form and is left alone; a non-equality comparison (>, <) or a non-min/max aggregate is not the antipattern.

cases.description: = (SELECT MIN(price) FROM products) selects the cheapest row by matching a scalar min subquery — ORDER BY price LIMIT 1 is idiomatic.
cases.sql: SELECT name FROM products WHERE price = (SELECT MIN(price) FROM products)

cases.description: = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees) selects the highest-paid row via a scalar max subquery — same antipattern on the max side.
cases.sql: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)

cases.description: The near-miss negative: a correlated subquery (its WHERE references the outer row's category) genuinely needs the subquery form — must NOT be flagged.
cases.sql: SELECT name FROM products p WHERE p.price = (SELECT MIN(p2.price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category)

cases.description: price > (SELECT AVG(price) ...) is a legitimate above-average filter, not a row-by-extreme match — not the antipattern.
cases.sql: SELECT name FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)

cases.description: A plain MIN aggregate as the answer (no equality-to-subquery) is fine here — the null_ordering check owns the unguarded-min hazard, not this one.
cases.sql: SELECT MIN(price) FROM products WHERE price IS NOT NULL
